title: Land Cessions and Indian Removal, 1784–1894
summary: Turn on one period at a time to watch American Indian land cessions spread across the United States, predict where the next ones will be, and explain why the 1830s cessions are where they are. The map is Charles Royce's record of cessions, so students also ask whose view it shows.
subject: History
time: About 60 minutes, or two parts: questions 1 to 4, then 5, 6 and the big question
studentLogin: Not needed to explore the map

map.about: This map shows the land the United States gained from American Indian nations by treaty, act of Congress or executive order between 1784 and 1894, from the records Charles Royce compiled for the federal government (published 1899). There is one layer for each period: before 1830, the 1830s and 1840 to 1894. Only the cessions dated before 1830 are on when the map opens; students turn on the later periods themselves. State names, cities and rivers are labeled above the colored areas. Each area's pop-up gives the nation named in the record, the date or dates, today's states and the nations that exist today, and most link to the treaty, statute or executive order.

layers.name: Cessions dated 1840 to 1894
layers.shows: Green areas: cessions with a date from 1840 to 1894. Off when the map opens.
layers.source: USDA Forest Service, from Charles C. Royce's maps and schedule (Bureau of American Ethnology, 1899)

layers.name: Cessions dated 1830 to 1839
layers.shows: Orange areas: cessions with a date in the 1830s, the decade of the Indian Removal Act. Off when the map opens.
layers.source: USDA Forest Service, from Charles C. Royce's maps and schedule (Bureau of American Ethnology, 1899)

layers.name: Cessions dated before 1830
layers.shows: Light blue areas: cessions with a date from 1784 to 1829.
layers.source: USDA Forest Service, from Charles C. Royce's maps and schedule (Bureau of American Ethnology, 1899)

knownIssues.note: Nations today reads "Not listed in this map's data." The Forest Service data has no present-day nation for any of the 13 Creek records. Question 6 uses it as a source question; the answer notes name nations that exist today.

The boundaries are coarse along rivers: Vicksburg falls just outside the cession Royce shows it in. No question depends on which side of a line a riverside town falls (checked 30 Oct 2026, maps/data/checks/).

knownIssues.where: Areas with more than one date
knownIssues.note: Royce lists every treaty that concerns an area, and the layers use any of its dates, so an area can appear in an earlier layer than its cession. Central Florida (Seminole) is light blue because the 1823 treaty set it aside as a reservation; it was ceded in 1832. Some Kansas areas carry the date they were assigned to a nation moved west. Reading the map and questions 3 and 4 say so.
Nations today lists the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians twice, spelled two ways; it is one nation.
No link to a treaty, statute or order in the pop-up: the Forest Service data has none.

compellingQuestion.en: How did the United States gain American Indian land between 1784 and 1894, and why did the pattern change in the 1830s?

questions.task: With only Cessions dated before 1830 on, name states where the United States had gained land, one big empty part of the country, and the gaps in the Southeast.
frontOfClass: Open The United States bookmark. Only Cessions dated before 1830 (light blue) is on.
Open the legend: light blue is Cessions dated before 1830.
Ask: name three states where the United States gained land before 1830, and one big part of the country with none.
Open The Southeast bookmark.
Ask: which states in the Southeast have gaps with no light blue?

steps.en: Find the light blue areas (Cessions dated before 1830) in the legend and on the map.
Open The Southeast bookmark and look for gaps: places in Mississippi, Alabama and Georgia with no light blue.

ask.en: (a) Name three states where the United States gained land before 1830. (b) Name one big part of the United States with no light blue. (c) Which Southeast states have gaps with no light blue?

answer.where: Cessions dated before 1830 layer, The United States bookmark. Light blue covers most of Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Missouri, Arkansas and Florida, much of Alabama, Georgia and Tennessee, southern Michigan, the south and west of Mississippi, parts of Pennsylvania and New York, and land west of Missouri and Arkansas (today's Kansas and Oklahoma).
answer.accept: (a) Any three of Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Missouri, Arkansas, Florida, Alabama, Georgia, Tennessee, Mississippi (the south and west), southern Michigan, Kansas or Oklahoma. (b) The West, the upper Great Lakes and upper Mississippi (Wisconsin, Minnesota, Iowa, northern Michigan), or the Atlantic coast. (c) Mississippi (north and center), Alabama (east-central and northeast) and Georgia (northwest).
answer.text: New England and the states from New Jersey to South Carolina are empty or nearly empty because Royce's record starts with the federal government in 1784: land taken in colonial times, or by the states, isn't on this map. Central Florida is light blue because an 1823 treaty set it aside as a Seminole reservation, not because it was ceded then (see question 4). Both are questions about the source, which question 6 comes back to.

questions.task: Before turning on the next layer, students predict where the cessions of the 1830s will be and give a reason. They write the prediction down first.
frontOfClass: Keep only Cessions dated before 1830 on.
Ask: where do you expect the cessions of the 1830s to be?
Ask: why there? Have students write the prediction down before anyone turns on the next layer.

steps.en: Keep only Cessions dated before 1830 on.
Look at the gaps you found in the Southeast, and at the empty parts east and west of the Mississippi River (the long river that runs down the middle of the country to the Gulf of Mexico).
Write your prediction before you turn on any other layer.

ask.en: Where do you expect the cessions of the 1830s to be? Why there?

fill.en: I predict the 1830s cessions will be in ______________ because ______________.

answer.accept: Any prediction with a reason drawn from question 1: for example, the empty pockets in the Southeast surrounded by earlier cessions, the land next to the Great Lakes, or the West. Predictions are checked in question 3, not marked right or wrong here.

questions.task: Turn on Cessions dated 1830 to 1839 and compare the orange areas with the prediction. Use The Southeast and The Old Northwest bookmarks.
frontOfClass: In Map layers, turn on Cessions dated 1830 to 1839 (orange).
Ask: name three states with orange areas. Was your prediction right?
Open The Southeast bookmark, then The Old Northwest (the Great Lakes states).
Ask: what happened to the gaps you found in the Southeast in question 1?

steps.en: In Map layers, turn on Cessions dated 1830 to 1839 (orange).
Open The Southeast bookmark, then The Old Northwest bookmark (the Great Lakes states).
Compare the orange areas (Cessions dated 1830 to 1839) with your prediction.

ask.en: (a) Name three states with orange areas (Cessions dated 1830 to 1839). (b) Was your prediction right? (c) What happened to the gaps you found in the Southeast in question 1?

answer.where: Cessions dated 1830 to 1839 layer, with The Southeast and The Old Northwest bookmarks. Orange fills most of the empty pockets in the Southeast: northern and east-central Mississippi, east-central and northeastern Alabama with strips along the Mississippi border, northwest Georgia, and corners of Tennessee and North Carolina. It also covers central Florida, which was already light blue. In the north it covers most of Wisconsin, much of Iowa, northern Michigan and northern Indiana. About four tenths of the orange is west of the Mississippi, in Iowa, Missouri, Kansas, Nebraska and Oklahoma.
answer.accept: (a) Any three of Mississippi, Alabama, Georgia, Wisconsin, Iowa, Michigan, Indiana, Florida, Kansas, Oklahoma, Missouri or Nebraska. (b) An honest comparison with the prediction. (c) The orange areas fill the gaps in Mississippi, Alabama and Georgia.
answer.text: Some orange areas in Kansas and Oklahoma were land assigned to nations moved west, which they ceded later; their pop-ups list more than one date. No question depends on them.

questions.task: Open orange cessions in the Southeast and read the nation, the date and the kind of document; use the Indian Removal Act (1830), in Before you start, to explain the pattern.
frontOfClass: Make sure Cessions dated 1830 to 1839 is on, and open The Southeast bookmark.
Click the large orange area in Mississippi, north-east of Jackson, and read the pop-up: the nation is the title, then the date, and the first link says what kind of document it is.
Click two more orange areas: in Alabama, between Birmingham and the Georgia line, north of Montgomery; and in the north-west corner of Georgia.
Ask: which nations, which years, and what kind of document?
Read Andrew Jackson's words in Before you start. Ask: how might the Indian Removal Act and Jackson's reason explain why these cessions came in the 1830s, and why here?

steps.en: Make sure Cessions dated 1830 to 1839 (orange) is on, and open The Southeast bookmark.
Click three orange areas: in Mississippi north-east of Jackson; in Alabama north of Montgomery, near the Georgia line; in the north-west corner of Georgia.
For each one, write the nation (the title of the pop-up), the date, and the words on the first link (for example Treaty text). You don't need to open the link.

ask.en: (a) Fill in the nation, date and link words for each area. (b) Read the Indian Removal Act and Jackson's words in Before you start. Why might these cessions have come in the 1830s, and why here?

answer.where: Cessions dated 1830 to 1839 layer, The Southeast bookmark, pop-ups. Mississippi, north-east of Jackson: Choctaw, September 27, 1830 (Today's states: Alabama, Mississippi). Alabama, north of Montgomery near the Georgia line: Creek, March 24, 1832. The north-west corner of Georgia: Cherokee, December 29, 1835 (Alabama, Georgia, North Carolina, Tennessee). Others students may open: Chickasaw, October 20, 1832 (northern Mississippi); Seminole, central Florida around Orlando, September 18, 1823 and May 9, 1832. Each of these first links reads Treaty text. A student who clicks Jackson itself gets a light blue Choctaw cession of 1820.
answer.accept: Connects the dates to the Indian Removal Act: after May 1830 the President could make removal treaties with nations east of the Mississippi, and within about five years the Choctaw, Creek, Chickasaw and Cherokee nations had ceded their remaining homelands in Mississippi, Alabama and Georgia. Explains why here with Jackson's own reason: he wanted the land between Tennessee and Louisiana opened to white settlement, and these were the nations' remaining lands, surrounded by land already ceded. Strong answers note that the map shows when and where, and the documents give the why.
answer.text: Two dates on one area don't always mean two cessions: Royce lists every treaty that concerns an area. The Seminole area in central Florida was set aside as a reservation in 1823 and ceded in 1832. The Treaty of New Echota (December 1835) was signed by the minority Treaty Party; Principal Chief John Ross, the Cherokee government and most Cherokees opposed it, and 3,352 Cherokees signed an 1836 petition asking the Senate not to ratify it (National Archives, DocsTeach). The National Archives says Jackson's administration negotiated almost 70 removal treaties, and nearly 50,000 people were moved to Indian Territory. Some people of each nation stayed in the Southeast: the Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians and the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians (both in the pop-ups' Nations today) and the Poarch Band of Creek Indians in Alabama live there today.

questions.task: Turn on Cessions dated 1840 to 1894 and describe how the pattern changed, using The Plains and the West bookmark.
frontOfClass: In Map layers, turn on Cessions dated 1840 to 1894.
Open The United States bookmark, then The Plains and the West.
Ask: where are most of the green areas (Cessions dated 1840 to 1894), and how is that different from the 1830s?
Ask: which parts of the country have no cessions at all, and why might that be?

steps.en: In Map layers, turn on Cessions dated 1840 to 1894 (green).
Open The United States bookmark, then The Plains and the West bookmark.

ask.en: (a) Where are most of the green areas (Cessions dated 1840 to 1894)? (b) Name one part of the United States with no cessions at all on this map.

answer.where: Cessions dated 1840 to 1894 layer. Green covers almost all of the West: the Plains, the Rocky Mountains, the Southwest, California and the Pacific Northwest, and Minnesota. It also covers most of today's Oklahoma, where nations moved from the East later ceded land again. Still empty or nearly empty: New England, New Jersey to South Carolina (apart from parts of Pennsylvania and New York), most of Kentucky, most of Louisiana, eastern Texas and part of North Dakota.
answer.accept: Says the cessions moved west of the Mississippi and across the whole West after 1840; notes the empty East and links it to the record starting in 1784.
answer.text: Eastern Texas is empty; central and western Texas have cessions by the Comanche, Kiowa and Apache (1865 to 1886). Where several layers overlap (Oklahoma, Kansas, Iowa) the colors mix: clicking shows each area's dates.

questions.task: Read the note at the end of a pop-up and the Nations today line for two cessions, including the Creek cession of 1832, and ask whose view of these transactions the map shows.
frontOfClass: Click the Cherokee cession in the north-west corner of Georgia. Scroll to the end of the pop-up and read the last sentence.
Ask: who recorded these cessions, and from whose records?
Click the Creek cession in Alabama, north of Montgomery, and read Nations today.
Ask: what is missing from the Creek pop-up?
Read the line from the 1836 Cherokee petition in question 6. Ask: how does it change how you read the Cherokee pop-up?

steps.en: Click the orange area in the north-west corner of Georgia (Cherokee). Scroll to the end of the pop-up and read the last sentence.
Click the orange area in Alabama north of Montgomery (Creek) and read Nations today.

ask.en: (a) Who recorded these cessions, and from whose records? (b) What is missing from the Creek pop-up? (c) In 1836, 3,352 Cherokees signed a petition saying the treaty was made "without any authority from the council or people of the Nation." How does that change how you read the Cherokee pop-up?

answer.where: Pop-up's last sentence: Royce compiled this from United States records (published 1899), so it shows how the federal government recorded the transaction, and the boundary is approximate. The Creek cession of March 24, 1832 reads "Not listed in this map's data." under Nations today.
answer.accept: (a) Charles Royce, from United States government records, published by the federal government in 1899. (b) A nation that exists today: the Muscogee (Creek) Nation in Oklahoma is one, and the Poarch Band of Creek Indians in Alabama another; the gap is in the modern data. (c) The pop-up records the Cherokee cession as a treaty, but the petition shows that many Cherokees said the people who signed it had no authority to speak for the nation, so the map gives the United States' side of a disputed agreement.
answer.text: The petition is in the National Archives (Records of the U.S. Senate); DocsTeach has the image and transcription. The layer was digitized by the USDA Forest Service, which says the data are for information only, not for deciding title or boundaries.

final.teacher: Students answer the compelling question with evidence from all three layers and at least two pop-ups, then write one "why" question the map raised for them. Accept answers that describe the pattern over time (the Ohio valley, much of the South and the land just west of the Mississippi before 1830; the Southeast and the upper Mississippi and Great Lakes in the 1830s; the West after 1840), connect the 1830s to the Indian Removal Act with dates from the pop-ups, and say that the map is a federal record. The students' own questions are a good place to start the next lesson, for example on the Trail of Tears.

student.en: Answer the big question, How did the United States gain American Indian land between 1784 and 1894, and why did the pattern change in the 1830s?, using evidence from all three layers and at least two pop-ups. Then write one "why" question this map raises for you.

objectives: Describe where the United States had gained American Indian land before 1830, using the Cessions dated before 1830 layer and the legend.
Make a prediction about the next period from the map, then turn on the 1830s layer and test it.
Read the nation, date and kind of document in the pop-ups of three 1830s cessions in the Southeast.
Explain the 1830s pattern in the Southeast using the Indian Removal Act (1830) as evidence.
Evaluate the map as a source: who recorded the cessions, when, and whose view is missing.
discussion: Your prediction in question 2: what did you base it on, and what did the 1830s layer show that you didn't expect?
The map shows where and when, but not why. What other evidence would you need to explain a single cession, such as the Cherokee cession of 1835?
Royce called these areas cessions. Is cession a fair word for all of them? What other words might the nations named in the pop-ups use?

differentiation.support: Do questions 1 and 3 from the front with the legend open, and point out the three places to click in question 4 (north-east of Jackson, north of Montgomery, the north-west corner of Georgia) on the projected map.
differentiation.stretch: Open the Treaty text link for the Cherokee cession of 1835 and find one article about moving west; compare it with what the pop-up and Before you start say.

assessment.evidence: Strong answers use all three layers in order (where light blue, orange and green fall), pop-up names and dates for at least two 1830s Southeast cessions (Choctaw, September 27, 1830; Creek, March 24, 1832; Cherokee, December 29, 1835), the Indian Removal Act and Jackson's reason, and the pop-up's note on who recorded the map.
assessment.exemplar: The United States gained American Indian land mostly by treaty, and the cessions moved across the map in a clear order. With only the light blue layer on, the cessions before 1830 cover Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Missouri and much of the lower South, but there are empty pockets in Mississippi, east-central Alabama and northwest Georgia. When I turned on the orange 1830s layer, those pockets filled in. The pop-ups show the Choctaw cession on September 27, 1830, the Creek on March 24, 1832 and the Cherokee on December 29, 1835, and each link says Treaty text. The Indian Removal Act of May 1830 let the President make removal treaties with nations east of the Mississippi, and Jackson wanted the land between Tennessee and Louisiana opened to settlement, so within five years the nations' remaining homelands in the Southeast were ceded. After 1840 the green layer covers almost the whole West. The pop-up note says Royce compiled the map from United States records, so it is the federal government's record. The 1836 Cherokee petition says the treaty was made without the authority of the nation, so the map gives one side of a disputed agreement. The Creek pop-up also leaves out a nation that exists today.

beforeYouStart.en: A treaty is a written agreement between nations. A cession is land a nation gives up, usually in a treaty. On May 28, 1830, President Andrew Jackson signed the Indian Removal Act. It let the President make treaties to move American Indian nations from east of the Mississippi River to land in the West. In December 1830, Jackson told Congress that removal meant "opening the whole territory between Tennessee on the north and Louisiana on the south to the settlement of the whites." The map comes from records Charles Royce made from government documents. The government published them in 1899.

readingTheMap.en: Light blue: cessions dated before 1830. Orange: 1830 to 1839. Green: 1840 to 1894. Only light blue is on at the start; turn on the others in Map layers when a question asks. Where layers overlap, the colors mix: click the area to read its dates. Some areas have two or more dates. The first date can be a treaty that kept the land for the nation, so read every date. Click an area to open its pop-up; scroll to see all of it.

reflection.en: Turning the layers on one at a time, what did you notice about how the cessions spread that you might have missed on a finished map?

teacherNotes.beforeClass: The map opens with only Cessions dated before 1830 on. Students turn on the 1830s layer in question 3 and the 1840 to 1894 layer in question 5; question 2's prediction works best before the later layers are on. State names, cities and rivers are labeled above the colored areas, and the steps use them to say where to click (for example, north-east of Jackson). The sheet names each layer by its date as well as its color.

misconceptions.claim: Empty parts of the map, such as New England and Virginia, were never American Indian land.
misconceptions.response: Royce's record starts in 1784. Land taken in colonial times, or by the states, isn't on this map.

misconceptions.claim: Two dates in a pop-up mean the land was ceded twice.
misconceptions.response: Royce lists every treaty that concerns an area. In central Florida, the 1823 treaty set the land aside as a Seminole reservation and the 1832 treaty ceded it.

misconceptions.claim: A cession means a nation chose to sell its land.
misconceptions.response: Many cessions were made under pressure or disputed; the map is the federal government's record of them, as the pop-up note says.

misconceptions.claim: A bigger colored area means more land was taken in that period.
misconceptions.response: The same land can appear in more than one layer: most of Oklahoma is light blue, orange and green, because Royce lists every treaty that concerns an area. The basemap's projection also makes northern areas look larger than southern ones.

Georgia is a resource only, and the Trail of Tears is planned for a later map).
